searchDocs.content: Development Basics Each Module is essentially a building block with properties that can communicate with other Modules. To specify a Module, you then have to provide three (3) main pieces of information: Manifest: The general information about the Module, e.g. name, descriptionProperties: The list of properties that the Module haveCode: Some sort of logic/code that will run Code Language​ The openexus specification is designed to be language agnostic. Each module is a "black box" where the internal logic should not matter. The openexus.com platform supports a variety of languages such as Javascript, Typescript, and Python, and new languages are added often. Counter Example​ This is a basic Module with a button that will increment a ((value)) property every time the button is clicked. manifest.yaml name: Counter description: Simple counter example. properties.yaml ui: datatype: html count: datatype: number default: 1 src/main.jsx function increment() { // Increment the value of ((count)) context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); } function render() { // Function that returns JSX can bind to // property of datatype `html` return ( <button on:click={increment}> Increment {context.get('count')} </button> ) } // Bind a function that returns JSX context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.title: Introduction
searchDocs.content: Introduction Welcome to Openexus! Openexus is as unified platform for building Modules and Applications with simplicity and ease. With just a few clicks or some simple AI description, the application of your dreams is ready to be explored and shared. The only thing it takes is imagination. Today, digital creations are made up of monolithic applications with thousands of lines code; hunderdeds of thousands of lines of code even. We believe that with a well designed building blocks concept we can design a world where creations are simple to build using with highly reusable blocks. These blocks can span multiple languages and frameworks and remove all the complex and esorteric programming concepts that get in the way. Tutorial​ If you have not yet tried it out, it might be beneficial for you to walk through the Openexus Tutorial once. Playgrounds​ To get a sense of using Modules and connecting them together, try out the Openexus Playground.If you is more interested in developing a Module, our Openexus Developer Playground is a good place to start. Here you can build out a custom Module and populate it however you want.That said, if you are more serious about your work, why not get started by creating an Openexus Account where you can create custom Modules and Applications and have them saved and persistent across device and sessions. We are currently waitlisting users but you can Join the Waitlist and hope we invite you soon. The Open Module Specification​ The core aspect of Openexus is the Module. A Module is functionally just a building block of some aspect of a software system. By creating and combining Modules together, either your own or those of others, we can build larger and more complex systems. Think of Open Module as a smart Lego block for digital creations. Just like Legos... Modules can snap (aka connect) with other Modules.Each Module can have different features (different properties).Connecting multiple Modules together will form a more complex and interesting creation. At the heart of a Module, is what we call the Open Module Specification. Features​ The Open Module Specification is designed with these principles in mind: Simple to use by non-coders;Programming language agnostic;Built to be highly reusable;Designed to be understood by AI. Core Concepts​ There are a few Core Concepts one should know to get going with Openexus. These are Modules;Instances;Properties;and Connections. We describe each of these below. Modules​ The primary building block of Openexus is the Module. A module is a building block (like Lego blocks) that allow users to piece them together to create interactive pages or applications. A Module can be as simple as a single function (e.g. age calculator) or as complex as an entire entity with complex visual and interactive elements (e.g. a map component). More fundamentally though, a Module is the description of a building block, the blueprint of it. It describes the module itself (the Manifest), the means of communication with the Module (the Properties), and the logic that is performed when the module is used or changes in some way (the Logic). We will go more into each of these concept in a minute. Instances​ An Instance is a running copy of a Module. If a Module is blueprint, an instance is a single implementation of that blueprint. If you think of a Module as a blueprint of a house, an Instance is the actual built house, a single stamped output of taking a blueprint and implementing against it. When you add a Module to an Openexus application, you are creating an Instance of that Module. Changes you make to that Instance are only applicable for that Instance and do not change the module itself. It is an important distinction to understand, the difference between a Module and an Instance. Properties​ Each module defines zero or more Properties. A Property is a single named data point of a Module. These data points each hold a specific value. The type of the value and what its is is entirely dependent on the Module being used. Connections​ Instances are tied to one another by a Connection. A Connection represents a binding between two specific Properties in two separate modules. You connect a Property on some Module to a Property on a different Module. When a Property changes on the first Module, the Property on the second Module is changed as well. We describe this as the Properties being "in-sync" meaning that what happens to one is reflected in the other.

searchDocs.title: Automatic Properties [Phase2]
searchDocs.content: Automatic Properties [Phase2] It is very common for your module to use dom elements and you want to allow the end-user to easily modify attributes via properties. For example, if you use <input>, you may want to surface ((on_key_up)) or ((on_blur)) triggers. <input config:bind /> // auto bind all <input config:bind={{ includes: ['on-blur'], excludes: ['on-change'] }} /> // includes and excludes <input config:bind={{ prefix: 'input', defaults: { border: 'border border-light', padding: 'p-2', 'border-radius': 'rounded', background: 'bg-light', }, }} // prefix port names <input bind:style /> // e.g. background, color, padding, margin, border, classes <input bind:properties /> // e.g. type, value, etc. <input bind:triggers /> // e.g. keyup, focus, etc. Supported elements​ divinputimgvideo

searchDocs.title: Using Modules
searchDocs.content: Using Modules Communication​ Nodes communicate to each other via connections between ((properties)). In general, when ((properties)) are connected, values are kept in-sync between them. For example, if we connect Input's ((value)) with Slider's ((number)), whenever the ((value)) or ((number)) changes, the other module ((value)) or ((number)) will also have the same value. On the Openexus platform, we do smart casting to make connection easy.

searchDocs.title: Frameworks Overview
searchDocs.content: Frameworks Overview Openexus support for JavaScript/TypeScript allows for the optional usage of several popular open-source JavaScript/TypeScript frameworks. You may choose which framework to use from the list of supported frameworks below. Some Modules do not even need a Framework at all. A Module only needs a Framework if it has some sort of visual output. Even if a Module has visual output, using a framework is entirely up to you. It should also be noted that Openexus supports ANY framework you might want to work with, so long as we support the underlying programming languages. We provided a number of helpers and documentation for the most common frameworks, but any framework that renders to the DOM and HTML is perfectly fine with us. The Framework you choose will dictate the way your module is setup. Please see the Frameworks section documentation for more details. While using a framework may be helpful for some, it is entirely optional as Openexus supports standard Javascript/TypeScript, HTML, CSS, and DOM manipulation. For JavaScript and Typsescript modules, Openexus suports the following frameworks: Standard/Vanilla JS: DocumentationSolid: DocumentationReact: DocumentationVue: DocumentationSvelte: Documentation

searchDocs.title: Characters Count
searchDocs.content: Characters Count A simple Module that counts the number of occurrences of a character in string. This Module has no UI elements. Features used in this example: Read and write values to properties using context.get() and context.set().Subscribe to changes on specific properties. Example​ manifest.yaml name: Characters Occurance description: Count the occurrence of a character in certain text. icon: mdi:counter properties.yaml string: datatype: text io: input required: true character: datatype: text io: input required: true count: description: The number of occurrence of a character in string. datatype: number io: output src/main.jsx let char = context.get('character'); let str = context.get('string'); function countCharacters() { let num = 0; let pos = str.indexOf(char); while (pos > -1) { pos = str.indexOf(char, pos + 1); num++; } context.set('count', num); } context.subscribe('string', (v) => { str = v; countCharacters(); }); context.subscribe('character', (v) => { char = v; countCharacters(); });

searchDocs.title: Quick Start
searchDocs.content: Quick Start Creating a Module​ Each Module is essentially a building block with Properties that can communicate with other Modules. A Module is a "black box" where the internal logic is completely hidden from another Module. Everything that a Module does, everything it allows other Modules to connect to, these things are entirely up to the Module author. To create a Module, we need these pieces of information: Manifest Declaration: The general information about the Module, e.g. name, description;Properties Declaration: The list of properties that the Module exposes;and Code: Optional code or logic that will execute on behalf of the Module. While it is entirely possible to create a Module with only a Manifest, Properties make the Module usable by others, and Code makes the Module more powerful and useful. Code & Programming Languages & Frameworks​ The Openexus Module Specification is designed to be language agnostic. As such, the programming language a Module uses is up to the Module author. The openexus.com platform supports a variety of programming languages such as Javascript, Typescript, and Python, and new languages are added often. Additionally, a programming language often has multiple frameworks that allow easier and faster software development. These frameworks are entirely dependent on the programming language being used. That said, Openexus supports a variety of frameworks for different programming languages. Which framework, if any, a Module uses is entirely up to the Module author. For more information regarding support programming languages and frameworks, please see the Openexus Module Specification > Code section. An Example Module​ This is a basic Module with a button that will increment a ((value)) Property every time the button is clicked. manifest.yaml name: Counter description: Simple counter example. properties.yaml ui: datatype: html count: datatype: number default: 1 src/main.jsx function increment() { // Increment the value of ((count)) context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); } function render() { // Function that returns JSX can bind to // property of datatype `html` return ( <button on:click={increment}> Increment {context.get('count')} </button> ) } // Bind a function that returns JSX context.set('ui', render); [TODO]: Update embed to be the code above Next Steps​ By now, you know the basics of a module creation! Examples is a good place to see how to create various different types of modules.Specification is a good place to learn about the complete specification of a module.Javascript/Typescript is a good starting point to learn more about using the SDK to create modules.

searchDocs.title: Vanilla / Standard / No Framework
searchDocs.content: Vanilla / Standard / No Framework One option for JavaScript/TypeScript development is to not use a framework at all and just relying on plain JavaScript/TypeScript, HTML, CSS, and DOM manipulation. To do so one must manually build out their DOM structure via JavaScript/TypeScript DOM calls and manually setup the details of the HTML. Setup and Usage​ NOTE: Because Vanilla JS/TS is not using a framework it requires less setup over other frameworks. To use Vanilla JS/TS... Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use react and Openexus together. Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/main.js // Create a render function function render() { // Your DOM setup and manipulation go here... } // Set the ((ui)) property to be the render function context.set('ui', context.render(render)) Example​

searchDocs.title: Writing Your First Module
searchDocs.content: Writing Your First Module To write your first Module, you will need to populate three things: The Manifest Declaration,the Properties Declaration,and the Code. Manifest Declaration​ The Manifest Declaration describes your Module from a high level point of view. Things like name, description, categories, and documentation all go in your Manifest. The values you enter here help guide other in finding and using your Module, so they are very important. For your first Module, let us keep this very simple: We will enter just a name and a description. manifest.yaml name: My First Module description: This is my very first module and I am super excited to see it work! Properties Declaration​ A Properties Declaration describes the data points a Module exposes. Some data points in a Module are internal and just for a Module to use. Others are external and intended for other Modules that interact with your Module to use. The Properties Declaration is where you describe these external data points. The Properties Declaration is made up of zero or more Property declarations. Each Property you want to expose is described here. For each Property you must specify at most a Property Key, but we also recommend you also provide a datatype. The Property Key is the name of the Property you will use to reference that Property whenever you want to interact with it. It is strongly encouraged that you use meaningful names that you can understand and that others will understand. Calling a Property a is not as helpful as calling is firstname. There are specific rules about what a Property Key must look like, so make sure to read Property Keys section of the Openexus Module Specification. properties.yaml ui: datatype: html count: datatype: number default: 1! Code​ The Code of a Module defines the logic of what happens when the Module is started and when the Module changes in some manner. Every Module executes its code when it is created each time, and that code may also specify additional points to execute as the Module changes. The details of this are up to you. The programming language and any framework a Module uses is up to you so long as Openexus supports it. For our first Module here, let us use JavaScript with the Solid framework. src/main.jsx function increment() { // Increment the value of ((count)) context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); } function render() { // Function that returns JSX can bind to // property of datatype `html` return ( <p>You have clicked the button {context.get('count')} times</p> <button on:click={increment}>Increment</button> ) } // Bind a function that returns JSX context.set('ui', render); Our First Module​

searchDocs.title: JavaScript/TypeScript Overview
searchDocs.content: JavaScript/TypeScript Overview Openexus is designed to use the language you want with the framework (or not) of your choice. As such, creating modules in Openexus is mostly programming language and framework agnostic. However, Openexus cannot support every language or every frameworks, so pleasr review our documnetation for usage and compatability. JavaScript and TypeScript are both fully supported by Openexus, including a complete API, a variety of popular frameworks, and suppport for external packages from NPM. Supported Frameworks​ Openexus support for JavaScript/TypeScript allows for the optional usage of several popular open-source JavaScript/TypeScript frameworks. You may choose which framework to use from the list of supported frameworks below. Some Modules do not even need a Framework at all. A Module only needs a Framework if it has some sort of visual output. Even if a Module has visual output, using a framework is entirely up to you. It should also be noted that Openexus supports ANY framework you might want to work with, so long as we support the underlying programming languages. We provided a number of helpers and documentation for the most common frameworks, but any framework that renders to the DOM and HTML is perfectly fine with us. The Framework you choose will dictate the way your module is setup. Please see the Frameworks section documentation for more details. While using a framework may be helpful for some, it is entirely optional as Openexus supports standard Javascript/TypeScript, HTML, CSS, and DOM manipulation. For JavaScript and Typsescript modules, Openexus suports the following frameworks: Standard/Vanilla JS: DocumentationSolid: DocumentationReact: DocumentationVue: DocumentationSvelte: Documentation Module Structure​ The following illustrates the recommended file and folder structure for a module. ./ manifest.yaml properties.yaml src/ main.js Component.js utils.js Entry Point​ All modules must have a main file. This is the code which is run when the module is instantiated. It can reference other files and the like, but all the logic starts here.

searchDocs.title: Solid
searchDocs.content: Solid Openexus JavaScript/TypeScript support provides the ability to use the Solid framework within a module. This provides the module with all the power of Solid, JSX/TSX, and Reactive programming. In Openexus this may be achieved in one of two ways: via the Openexus Solid Helper,or, Manually Do it Yourself. Openexus Helper SDK​ The Solid Helper SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using Solid, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. To use Solid and the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript Solid Helper SDK... Import Framework and the SDK;Initialize the SDK;Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use Solid and Openexus together. There may be additional things to do to work with Openexus items within Solid, so make sure to read the Framework Specific Documentation below. Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as solidWeb from 'solid-js/web'; import * as solid from 'solid-js'; import { init } from 'openexus/solid'; Initialize the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx init(context, solid, solidWeb); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base Solid component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/main.jsx // Create a render function function SomeComponent() { return ( <p>Hello world!</p> ); } // Set the UI property to the Component. context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent)); // alt Example​ In order to do this Openexus requires the usage of the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript Solid SDK. The SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using Solid, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the Solid library without using the Openexus Solid Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus Solid Helper SDK, one must manually createRoot and render on the element when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.ts import { render } from "solid-js/web" import SolidComponent from './SolidComponent.jsx'; context.set('ui', (el) => render(SolidComponent, el)); Property References​ Without using the Openexus Solid Helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/SolidComponent.tsx import { useState, useRef, useEffect, createElement } from 'react'; function SolidComponent() { const [count, setCount] = createSignal(context.get('count')); onMount(() => { context.subscribe('count', (v) => { setCount(v); }); }); createEffect(() => { context.set('count', count()) }) return ( <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)} class='bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white py-2 px-4 rounded' > {`Count is ${count()}`} </button> ); } Framework Specifics​ Using the Solid framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular Solid, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property must be obtained from Openexus. The SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates a useable reactive signal from it. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => [getter, setter] Usage: const [count, setCount] = context.use('count');

searchDocs.title: Gallery
searchDocs.content: Gallery A gallery Module that renders connected UIs. Features used in this example: Example on how to use Slots and the [html] Data Type. Example​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid A gallery module that renders a connected UI without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: Gallery description: A gallery module that renders connected UI. properties.yaml ui: datatype: html slot: datatype: [html] src/main.jsx import { For, Show } from "@modules-js/components"; // This render function simply renders each connected UI // in a staggered way function render() { return ( <Show when={context.getExtended('slot').length > 0} fallback={<div>No UIs connected to slot!</div>} > <div style={{ position: 'relative' }}> <For each={context.getExtended('slot')}> {(ui, index) => ( <> <div>{context.data?.()}</div> </> )} </For> </div> </Show> ); } // Bind a function that returns JSX context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.title: Svelte
searchDocs.content: Svelte Openexus JavaScript/TypeScript support provides the ability to use the Svelte framework within a module. This provides the module with all the power of Svelte, JSX/TSX, and Reactive programming. In Openexus this may be achieved in one of two ways: via the Openexus Svelte Helper,or, Manually Do it Yourself. Openexus Helper SDK​ The Svelte Helper SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using Svelte, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. To use Svelte and the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript Svelte Helper SDK... Import Framework and the SDK;Initialize the SDK;Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use Svelte and Openexus together. There may be additional things to do to work with Openexus items within Svelte, so make sure to read the Framework Specific Documentation below. Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as svelteStore from 'svelte/store'; import * as svelte from 'svelte'; import { init } from 'openexus/svelte'; Initialize the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx init(context, svelte, svelteStore); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base Svelte component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/SomeComponent.svelte <p> Hello world! </p> src/main.jsx // Set the UI property to the Component. import SomeComponent from './SomeComponent.svelte'; context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent));`, Example​ Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the Svelte library without using the Openexus Svelte Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus Svelte Helper SDK, one must manually pass in the element through new SvelteComponent() when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.ts import SvelteComponent from './SvelteComponent.svelte'; context.set('ui', (el) => new SvelteComponent({ target: el })); Property References​ Without using the Openexus Svelte Helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/SvelteComponent.vue <script> import { onMount } from 'svelte'; import { writable } from 'svelte/store'; const count = writable(context.get('count')); onMount(() => { context.subscribe('count', (v) => { count.set(v); }); }); count.subscribe((value) => { context.set('count', value) }) function onClick() { countWritable.set(count + 1); } </script> <button on:click={onClick} class='bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white py-2 px-4 rounded' >{`Count is ${count}`}</button> Framework Specifics​ Using the Svelte framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular Svelte, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property must be obtained from Openexus. The SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates an object which allows setting the value and subscribing to changes on the value. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => svelteSetter Usage: let count = undefined; // create our get value const setCount = context.use('count'); // get out setter from Openexus setCount.subscribe((value)=>count=value); // Setup a function to update our get value when the setter is invoked. Because of the manner in which Svelte makes getters just local variables, we need to create a local variable for count let count = undefined; and then we need to update it any time its associated setter is updated: setCount.subscribe((value)=>count=value);. The object returned by context.use() is called a svelteSetter. It has two functions: svelteSetter.set(value): Sets the value of this item.svelteSetter.subscribe(f): Executes the given function f whenever svelteObject.set() is called.

searchDocs.title: Actions & Triggers
searchDocs.content: Actions & Triggers Actions and Triggers are the yin and yang of a Module, the push and pull of it. Actions are used to perform some behavior on a Module, to make it do something that the Module is capable of doing. Triggers are used to announce when a Module changes in a noteworthy way that in which other Modules would be interested. Together Actions and Triggers work together to announce changes and respond to those changes. Actions​ An Action is a Property with a Data Type of action. Actions are code that run when activated. They can be activated manually, or by being connected to a Trigger. The code associated with an action is a function that is set as a value to that action, as shown here: properties.yaml someAction: datatype: action src./main.js context.set('someAction', ()=>{ ... code to be executed on action invocation ... }); Setup an action​ To bind a function to an action property, simply call context.set(). Tip: You can manually call it by clicking on the "Set Description" dropdown on the module and click "Run Action" main.js context.set('send_email', () => { // Send email... }); Run an action​ Use the context.run() to execute an Action Property. Since we are developing the module, calling run may seem strange, but it is useful for testing and a few edge cases. main.js context.run('send_email'); Additionally, the concept of running an action makes more sense when you consider the need to execute an action on another instance's context, instead of the context of the module you are writing. main.js const instance = context.getInstance('9a3b8b8d-18e2-4951-a7cc-de8ff5dd42fd'); instance.run('send_sms'); Triggers​ A Trigger is a Property that is used to notify connected instances of some event. An event can be anything you want it to be. Events are typically due to some change in the Module like a mouse click or a photo taken. It depends on the Module and the use casebu t is entirely up to you when to use a trigger. Typcially we call the execution of a Trigger a "firing". So we tend to say "fire a trigger" to describe this process. Triggers my be connected to Actions such that when the connected Trigger fires, the connected Action is run. Firing a Trigger​ To fire off a Trigger property, simply call the context.trigger() function as shown here... main.js context.trigger('my_trigger');

searchDocs.title: ContextObject
searchDocs.content: ContextObject Before we talk about the Context Object, a quick review of what Modules and Instances are is in order. A Module is the definition and all the bits necessary for the Module to be executed. An instance is a single execution of a Module. For example, if one has an Input Module and ran it two separate times, they would have to separate Instances, one for each execution. When we are writing a Module, the context object that we often work with, is the running instance. So in our prior example of two Input Instances, each has its own context. Using the ContextObject​ The Context Object is available in your code as the context varaible. All of the members and methods described below are executed from the context object. For example, if we wanted to get a property value of the currently executing instancem we would do so by calling `context.get(). ContextObject Members​ ContextObject Methods​ use(...args: unknown[]) => unknown Used for frameworks to obtain a reactive pass through to instance properties. For example., if you are working with a framework like React, you might use it to get a getter/setter for a property. The getter/setter is a react store and behaves as expected of a react store. getModule() => ModuleObject Returns a ModuleObject that contains all the pertinent details about the parent Module for the current instance. getProperty(propertyKey: string) => PropertyObject Returns a PropertyObject that contains all the pertient details about that Property. It should be noted that a PropertyObject is different than a Property Value that represents what is currently stored in the property. The PropertyObject is all the details about the Property itself. trigger(propertyKey: string, event: unknown) => void Used to fire a Trigger event for the given propertyKey. The event object passed to this function will be provided as the event argument to down-stream trigger receivers. run(propertyKey: string, ...args: unknown[]) => void Used to execute an Action for the given propertyKey. Any additional arguments passed to the run function will be passed to the Action execution. get(propertyKey: string) => unknown Returns the current value of the given propertyKey. set(propertyKey: string, value: unknown) => void Sets the current value of the given propertyKey to value. Subscriptions, effects, and related signals bound to propertyKey will trigger after this value is updated. update(propertyKey: string, updateFunction: Function) => void Updates the current value of the given propertyKeys based on the return result of the updateFunction function. The updateFunction function has the following signature: <updateFunction> = (oldValue) => newValue mutate(propertyKey: string, mutator: Function) => void Updates the current value of the given propertyKeys based on the return result of the mutateFunction function. The mutateFunction function has the following signature: <mutateFunction> = (oldValue) => newValue subscribe(propertyKey: string | string[], handler: Function) => void Subscribe to notification when the given propertyKey (or propertyKeys) is changed. The handler is executed any time the propertyKey (or set of propertyKeys) changes. The handler function has the following signature: <handler function> = (newValue: unknown, oldValue: unknown, propertyKey: string) => void subscribeAll(handler: Function) => void Subscribe to ALL notificatioError: 'error', Warning: 'warning', Success: 'success', Info: 'info', Fetching: 'fetching', Fetched: 'fetched', Loading: 'loading', Loaded: 'loaded',ns when ANY property for the current instance is changed. The handler function has the follow signature: <handler function> = (newValue: unknown, oldValue: unknown, propertyKey: string) => void unsubscribe(propertyKey: string | string[], handler?: Function) => void Unsubscribe from notification when a property changes. One may specify a specific propertyKey or an array of propertyKeys to unsubscribe from. If a handler function is given unsubscribe will only occur on notifications that specifically match the given handler. Because functions are passed by reference in JavaScript/TypseScript this must be a referntial match and not a content match. onCleanup(handler: Function) => void Subscribe to receive notification when the Cleanup lifecycle event occurs. The given handler will be executed when this occurs. Note that the Cleanup lifecycle event IS NOT garaunteed to run. The handler function has the following signature: <handler function> = () => void notify(state:string, reason: string) => void Used to visually notify an instance that it is in a given state for a given reason. The possible state values are given below. If an invalid state is given, the notification WILL NOT be displayed. Possible states are: errorwarningsuccessinfofetchingfetchedloadingloaded

searchDocs.title: React
searchDocs.content: React Openexus JavaScript/TypeScript support provides the ability to use the React framework within a module. This provides the module with all the power of React, JSX/TSX, and Reactive programming. In Openexus this may be achieved in one of two ways: via the Openexus React Helper,or, Manually Do it Yourself. Openexus Helper SDK​ The React Helper SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using React, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. To use React and the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript React Helper SDK... Import Framework and the SDK;Initialize the SDK;Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use React and Openexus together. There may be additional things to do to work with Openexus items within React, so make sure to read the Framework Specific Documentation below. Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as reactDom from 'react-dom/client'; import react from 'react'; import { init } from 'openexus/react'; Initialize the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx init(context, react, reactDom); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base React component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/main.jsx // Create a render function function SomeComponent() { return ( <p>Hello world!</p> ); } // Set the UI property to the Component. context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent)); // alt Example​ Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the React library without using the Openexus React Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus React Helper SDK, one must manually createRoot and render on the element when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.tsx import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'; import ReactComponent from './ReactComponent.jsx'; context.set('ui', (el) => createRoot(el).render(ReactComponent())); Property References​ Without using the Openexus React Helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/ReactComponent.tsx import { useState, useRef, useEffect, createElement } from 'react'; function ReactComponent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(context.get('count')); useEffect(() => { context.subscribe('count', (v) => { setCount(v); }); }, []); useEffect(() => { context.set('count', count) }, [count]); return ( <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)} class='bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white py-2 px-4 rounded' > {`Count is ${count}`} </button> ); } Framework Specifics​ Using the React framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular React, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property must be obtained from Openexus. The Helper SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates a useable reactive signal from it. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => [getter, setter] Usage: const [count, setCount] = context.use('count');

searchDocs.title: JavaScript/TypeScript SDK Overview
searchDocs.content: JavaScript/TypeScript SDK Overview Openexus provides a SDK that sits between Openexus and your code. The SDK provides access to modules, instances, properties, etc. Basically, everything in Openexus can be found via the SDK. Context​ The SDK is exposed as the context global variable in your code. You can use this context object for a variety of purposes such as adding an instance of a module, accessing properties on the module, getting notified when something changes in Openexus, or execute an action. src/main.js // read the value of a property context.get('foo'); // set the value of a property context.set('foo', 'bar'); // set foo === bar // get notified when something changes context.subscribe('foo', (value,key) => { ... do something magical ... }); etc... There's a lot of things you can do, so please read the documentation below to find out more about context and how to access specific things... More about... ModuleObjectInstanceObjectPropertyObject Specific Things on might want to do... Read/Write property valuesSubscribe to property changesWork with Actions & TriggersUnderstand a Module LifecycleImport PackagesModule notifications

searchDocs.title: Dynamic Properties [Phase2]
searchDocs.content: Dynamic Properties [Phase2] Consider the last word of the below sentence. What does that mean? You can create properties dynamically during runtime too. Consider only doing this for properties that are truly dynamic. Visibility​ If a propery should be set/shown, the property should be available and not hidden. When to use dynamic properties?​ Sometimes you mey need to add/remove properties depending of the data. This is called Dynamic Properties where you create properties based on some other input property. An example of this is Text Templating where the properties you create are based on some text string. Imagine the template string "The {adjective} fox {verb} the lazy dog.". {adjective} and {verb} are properties you want to dynamically generate as the template string changes. Limitations:​ Makes discovery via Add Modules harder. Add a new property​ context.addProperty({ key: 'dynamic_key', datatype: 'text' }); Remove a property​ You can only remove dynamically created properties. context.removeProperty('dynamic_key'); Hide a property​ effect(() => { // property ((max)) is only shown when ((type)) is number context.getProperty('max').set('hidden', context.get('type') === 'number'); context.hideProperty('max', context.get('type') === 'number'); }); Templated dynamic properties​ const dynamicProperties = context.addPropertiesFromTemplate( 'greetings_template', 'Hello {{first name}} {{last name}}!', { description: '{name} for template', }, '/{{[\s\S]+}}/' ); effect(() => { dynamicProperties.forEach((p) => { console.log(p.getData()); }); }); // return reactive store of array of properties objects effect(() => { const dynamicProperties = context.addPropertiesFromTemplate( 'template', $.get('template'), { description: '{name} for template', default: '' }, '/{{[\s\S]+}}/' ); dynamicProperties.forEach((p) => { $.set('result', $.get('template').replaceAll(/{{[\s\S]+}}/, p.getData())); }); });

searchDocs.title: InstanceObject
searchDocs.content: InstanceObject A InstanceObject represents a single execution of a Module and contains all the details about that execution including things like proprties, connections, triggers, and actions.The InstanceObject provides a way to work with these things and change them. Manipulating these things only effects the given instance; multiple instance of the same module each have their own InstanceObjects one can execute against. We get the current context's InstanceObject using context.getInstance(). We can also get other InstanceObjects for any other instance so long as we know the instance uuid using context.getInstance(<instance uuid>). getInstance() has the following signature: getInstance(instanceId?: string) => InstanceObject InstanceObject Members​ <instance object>.id => string Returns the identifying UUID for this instance. Some times this is called the InstanceId. <instance object>.modulePid => string Returns the Module PID for this instance. A Module PID is a reference to the Parent Module. The Module PID and the version are the minimum requirements for identifying a Module within Openexus. <instance object>.moduleReleaseId => string Returns the moduleReleaseId, which is a UUID that points to a specific Module PID and version for a Module. <instance object>.createdAt => Date Returns the Date representing when the instance was initially created. <instance object>.updatedAt => Date Returns the Date representing when the instance was last updated. <instance object>.isRoot => boolean Returns true if this module is the Root Instance in the current module context. InstanceObject Methods​ The InstanceObject contains the following methods: Needs more <instance object>.get(propertyKey: string) => unknown Returns the value of the given propertyKey at this point in time. <instance object>.set(propertyKey: string, value: unknown) => void Sets the value of the given propertyKey. <instance object>.trigger(triggerKey: string, event?: Event) => void Fires the given Trigger named triggerKey with the optional event details. <instance object>.run(actionKey: string, ...args: unknown[]) => void Executes the given Action named actionKey with the optional args. <instance object>.subscribe(propertyKey: string, handler: Function) => void Subscribes to receive notifications when the given propertyKey is changed. When the propertyKey is change the given hanlder function is executed. <instance object>.subscribeAll(handler: Function) => void Subscribes to receive notifications when ANY property of this instance is changed. <instance object>.unsubscribe(propertyKey: string, handler: Function) => void Unsubscribe from receiving notifications when the given propertyKey is changed. The passed function must match the original function passed as the argument to subscribe(). <instance object>.unsubscribeAll() => void Unsubscribe from receiveing notifications when ANY property of the current instance is changed. The passed function must match the original function pssed as the argument to subscribeAll(). Examples​ Current Instance​ // Without passing in any id, getInstance will get the current instance object const instance = context.getInstance();

searchDocs.title: ModuleObject
searchDocs.content: ModuleObject A ModuleObject represents the parent module of an Instance. Because an Instance is the running execution of a Module, the ModuleObject is all the definitions and bits that make a Module and allow it to executed. This includes things like name, icon, screenshots, code, etc. Most of the time the Module itself is not really important, but on occasion it can be. Thus, the ModuleObject provides a way to work with a Module. We get the parent module for the current context instance using context.getModule(). We can also get the module for any other instance using <instance object>.getModule(). getModule() has the following signature: getModule() => ModuleObject ModuleObject Members​ The ModuleObject contains no members. ModuleObject Methods​ The ModuleObject contains the following methods: The following methods are available: <module object>.getName() => string Returns the module name, as a string. <module object>.getIcon() => string Returns the URL or Module Icon identifier to the user. Openexus supports a variety of Icon Identifiers from various open-source icon sets. See Iconify.design for examples. <module object>.getDescription() => string Return the description of a module. A module description is tells users what the module does, usually in a few short sentances. It describes the purpose of the module, but not necessarily how the user uses it. <module object>.getDocumentation() => string Return the documentation of a module. A module documentation is tells users how to use the module and provides details about how the module works. Documenation is in Markdown format, so displaying the documentation of a module may require usage of a Markdown viewer. Fortunately, Openexus has several Markdown viewer modules and they are easy to use. <module object>.getPlatform() => string Returns the platform/framework that a module uses. Largely the platform/framework of a module is only important for Openexus when the module's code is compiled and run. <module object>.getCategories() => string[] Returns an array of the categories of a module. Each module may have up to two (2) categories and each category may have a single nested levels of a category of the form <primary category>/<secondary category>. <module object>.getKeywords() => string[] Returns an array of the keywords of a module. Each module may have up to five (5) keywords. <module object>.getThumbnail() => string Returns the URL or relative file path of a thumbnail image for the given module. <module object>.getScreenshots() => string[] Returns an array of URL or relative file paths of screenshot images for the given module. Examples​

searchDocs.title: Counter
searchDocs.content: Counter Render a button that when clicked, increments a value. Features used in this example: Reading and writing values to properties (context.get and context.set).Render UI elements using different frameworks. Example​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid Simple counter button example without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: Counter (JavaScript) description: An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. categories: starter/javascript,starter/vanilla keywords: starter,javascript,vanilla,counter icon: logos:javascript properties.yaml ui: datatype: html count: datatype: number description: The number of times the button has been clicked since this application was started. This represents using a simple Property in the Openexus system. default: 1 src/main.js /** * An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple * button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. */ let button; // Define a render function to return our HTMLElement to display. function render() { // Create the element. button = document.createElement('button'); // Populate the element. button.innerHTML = `Count is ${context.get('count')}`; // Openexus components use tailwind by default, but you can define CSS // classes and styles in your preferred manner. button.classList.add('bg-blue-500', 'hover:bg-blue-700', 'text-white', 'py-2', 'px-4', 'rounded'); // For our button we want to mutate our count state when it is clicked. button.addEventListener('click', (value) => { context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); }); return button; } // Register to be notified when ((count)) changes. context.subscribe('count', (value) => { if (button) button.innerHTML = `Count is ${value}`; }); // Set our render function to the ((ui)) property for rendering. context.set('ui', context.render(render));

searchDocs.title: Lifecycle
searchDocs.content: Lifecycle A lifecycle describes the process your module goes through when used. Generally speaking a module goes through four phases, each a part of its lifecycle: Cleanup - When the module loaded by the subsystem and ready to be removed. Cleanup Lifecycle Event​ When a module is dispose entirely by the current system. This Lifecylce event is not garaunteed to occur. main.tsx context.onCleanup(() => { // When a module is cleaned up console.log('cleanup module') });

searchDocs.title: Vue
searchDocs.content: Vue Openexus JavaScript/TypeScript support provides the ability to use the Vue framework within a module. This provides the module with all the power of Vue, JSX/TSX, and Reactive programming. In Openexus this may be achieved in one of two ways: via the Openexus Vue Helper,or, Manually Do it Yourself. Openexus Helper SDK​ The Vue Helper SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using Vue, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. To use Vue and the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript Vue Helper SDK... Import Framework and the SDK;Initialize the SDK;Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use Vue and Openexus together. There may be additional things to do to work with Openexus items within Vue, so make sure to read the Framework Specific Documentation below. Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as vue from 'vue'; import { init } from 'openexus/vue'; Initialize the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx context = init(context, vue); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base Vue component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/SomeComponent.vue <template> <p> Hello world! </p> </template> src/main.jsx // Set the UI property to the Component. import SomeComponent from './SomeComponent.vue'; context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent));`, Example​ Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the Vue library without using the Openexus React Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus Vue helper SDK, one must manually createApp and mount on the element when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.ts import { createApp } from 'vue'; import VueComponent from './VueComponent.vue'; context.set('ui', (el) => createApp(VueComponent).mount(el)); Property References​ Without using the Openexus Vue helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/helper.ts import { ref, watch, onUnmounted } from 'vue'; function usePropertyRef(propertyName) { const propertyRef = ref(context.get(propertyName)); let isInternalUpdate = false; // Watch for local changes and update the context const stopWatch = watch(propertyRef, (newValue) => { if (!isInternalUpdate) { isInternalUpdate = true; context.set(propertyName, newValue); isInternalUpdate = false; } }); // Subscribe to external changes const unsubscribe = context.subscribe(propertyName, (newValue) => { if (!isInternalUpdate) { isInternalUpdate = true; propertyRef.value = newValue; isInternalUpdate = false; } }); // Cleanup onUnmounted(() => { stopWatch(); unsubscribe(); }); return propertyRef; } src/VueComponent.vue <script setup> import { usePropertyRef } from './helper.ts'; const count = usePropertyRef('count'); // returns a ref function onClick() { count.value = Math.random(); } </script> <template> <button @click="onClick">Count: {{ count }}</button> </template> Framework Specifics​ Using the Vue framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular Vue, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property reference must be obtained from Openexus. The SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates an reference to that object which can be interacted with to get and set the value. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => vueReference Usage: const countRef = context.use('count'); const foo = countRef.value; // getter countRef.value = 123; // setter

searchDocs.title: Overview
searchDocs.content: Overview Python modules are experimental If your module is going to be used in a web/browser environment, it is best to write the module in Javascript for performance reason. However, you can choose to write modules in Python if that is your preference. Considerations​ Currently our Python SDK is more limited than Javascript's.When your Python code is used on a web environment, the module will be evaluated in via a web assembly (WASM) wrapper.There will be some performance hit.You can import the most common Python libraries. However, libraries that require hardware cannot be imported.The wrapper will be Pyodide.

searchDocs.title: Read and Write Property Values
searchDocs.content: Read and Write Property Values Modules have properties to which one can read or write a value. It is the most common and basic task when developing a module. Fortunately, it is also incredibly easy. Read a property value​ The simpliest way to read data from a property is to use context.get('<property_name>'). For example... properties.yaml count: datatype: number default: 1 main.js console.log('Count is', context.get('count')); output Count is 1 Write value to a property​ Writing values to a property is also fairly simple, but for more complex values may require a bit more. Primative data types such as test, number, and boolean are easy. More complex data types like arrays and object require a little more thought, although it depends largely on what is being accomplished. Primitive values​ The recommended and simpliest way to write a new primatives value to a property is to use context.set('{property_name}', {value}). As shown here... main.js console.log('Count before write is', context.get('count')); context.set('count', 2); // set value to a property console.log('Count after write is', context.get('count')); output Count before write is 1 Count after write is 2 Update values​ Optionally, if you need to reference the prior value as part of writing a value, it is better to use context.update(). context.update() has the form context.update(<property name>, <update function>). Here's an example: main.js console.log('Count before update is', context.get('count')); context.update('count', (prev) => prev + 1); console.log('Count after update is', context.get('count')); Update object values​ If you are working with objects, you can also do fine-grain updates using context.mutate. Fine-grain mutations are preferred in reactive systems because we can reactivitly update the other connected properties in a fine-grained manner; meaning we can only update the part that changed, as opposed to the whole object. context.mutate() has the form context.mutate(<property name>, <mutate function>). Here's an example usage: main.js context.mutate('obj', (obj) => { obj.list[0] = '123'; obj.list.push(456); });

searchDocs.title: Read and Write Data
searchDocs.content: Read and Write Data Reading and writing data to properties on the node is the most common and basic task you may need to develop a module. Read a property value​ The recommended and simpliest way to read data from a property is to use context.get('{property_name}'). properties.yaml count: datatype: number default: 1 main.py print(f"read value: {context.get('count')}") output Count is 1 Write value to a property​ Primitive values​ The recommended and simpliest way to write a new value to a property is to use context.set('{property_name}', {value}). main.py print(f"Count is {context.get('count')}") context.set('count', 2) # set value to a property print(f"Count is {context.get('count')}") output Count is 1 Count is 2 Update values [?]​ If you need to reference the previous value, you can use context.update(). main.js context.update('count', (prev) => prev + 1); Update object values [?]​ If you are working with objects, you can also do fine-grain updates using context.mutate. Fine-grain mutations are preferred because we can reactivitly update the other connected properties in a fine-grained manner. main.js context.mutate((obj) => { obj.list[0] = '123' obj.list.push(456) });

searchDocs.title: Subscriptions
searchDocs.content: Subscriptions You can easily listen to changes to properties by using the provided subscribe function. Single Subscription​ To listen to a property change, simply call subscribe with the property key and the callback. main.py def value_changed(value): print(f"Count updated to {value}") context.subscribe('count', value_changed) Multiple Subscriptions [?]​ If you need to subscribe to mutliple properties at once, you can pass in an array of port keys. function callbackFn(path, value) { // should return cell instead of path? } context.subscribe(['property1', 'property2', ...], callbackFn); // subscribe to multiple ports Subscribe to all properties [?]​ This is useful if you have dynamic ports and you do know the port name ahead of time. function callbackFn(path, value) { // should return cell instead of path? } context.subscribeAll(callbackFn);

searchDocs.title: Styling
searchDocs.content: Styling Openexus suports two different styling options when working in JavaScript/TypeScript: Tailwind and imported CSS/SCSS/SASS/LESS, whichever Styling library is prefered for module development. All Styling options work with all JavaScript/TypeScript supported JavaScript/TypeScript frameworks. Tailwind Styling​ Tailwind is supported out of the box. Most Tailwind classes are supported and enabled on all frameworks. For more information on tailwind, please visit: https://tailwindcss.com/ Tailwind Example​ <div class='p-4 bg-blue-200'>Hello World!</div> Imported CSS Styling​ You can also import a CSS file in your module file structure. In addition to supporting CSS, Openexus also support SCSS, SASS, and LESS CSS formatting. CSSSCSSSASSLESS src/styles.css button { font: 100% Helvetica, sans-serif; background: #ff9900; } src/main.js import "./styles.css"; function render(element) { const node = document.createElement('button'); node.innerHTML = 'Click me!'; element.appendChild(node); } context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.content: categories The categories Manifest field is used to determine how to organize Modules when looking for a module in Openexus. A Module may specify up to two categories, comma seperated. searchDocs.title: Notifications
searchDocs.content: Notifications Sometimes it is helpful to convey the state of a module such as progress, warnings, or errors. This is called Module Notification and it is very simple to do. The context.notify() function allows your to specify a notification state, and a notification message to display. context.notify() has the following signature: context.notify(<state>, <message>); Where state is one of the Notification State values shown below, and message is any string of text you want to display. Notification States​ The following notification states are supported: success - Indicates some successful action or opertion.warning - Indicaes the module is in a warning state and needs attention.error - Indicates the module is in an error state and failing to execute for some reason.info - Indicates some information to the module user.fetching - Indicates the module is fetching data from an external source.fetched - Indicates the module completed fetching data from an external source.loading - Indicates some portion of the module is in the loading state.loaded - Indicates the the module has loaded completely. NOTE: Internally Openexues does not use the module notification to indicate if a module is loaded or not. loading and loaded are provided purely for module developers to use. NOTE: Any other state value that is not described above will result in no notification shown. Examples​ src/main.ts context.notify('error', 'Error occured!'); context.notify('warning', 'Authentication may be required'); context.notify('success', 'Success!'); context.notify('info', 'Parsing data'); context.notify('fetching', 'Downloading data...'); context.notify('fetched', 'Data downloaded!'); context.notify('loading', 'Calculating...'); context.notify('loaded', 'Done processing!'); Example​ src/main.ts setTimeout(() => { context.notify('fetching', 'Fetching data...'); const response = new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(() => resolve({'github': 'results'}), 3000); }) if (!response.ok) { response.then((result) => { context.set('githubIssues', result); context.notify('fetched', 'Data Fetched!'); }) } else { context.notify('error', 'Error Fetching Data.'); } }, 1000)

searchDocs.title: PropertyObject
searchDocs.content: PropertyObject Instances have zero or more properties. Each property is represented by a property object. We can use these Property Objects to manipulate the property and the current instance. NOTE: A PropertyObject is different than a Property Value. A PropertyObject describes the property itself, while a Property Value is the value a property contains. The access a Property Value use the context.get() method. Getting the PropertyObject​ The PropertyObject for any property is exposed via a call to context.getProperty() or a call to <instance object>.getProperty(). These calls return a PropertyObject if the given property is found, or undefined if not. getProperty() (both the context version and the InstanceObject version) has the following signature: getProperty(propertyKey: string) => PropertyObject | undefined PropertyObject Members​ PropertyObject has no members. PropertyObject Methods​ <property object>.get() => unknown Get the value for the current property. <property object>.set(value: unknown) => void Set the value of the current property. <property object>.update(updateFunction: Function) => void update the value of the current property. The updateFunction function has the following signature: <updateFunction> = (oldValue) => newValue <property object>.subscribe(handler: Function) => void Subscribe to notifications when the current property is changed. The handler is executed any time the current property changes. The handler function has the following signature: <handler function> = (newValue: unknown, oldValue: unknown, propertyKey: string) => void <property object>.remove() => void Remove the current property from its parent instance. <property object>.hide() => void Hide the current property from its parent instance. <property object>.show() => void Unhide the current property from its parent instance. <property object>.getHidden() => boolean Returns true if the current property is hidden. <property object>.setHidden(hidden: boolean) => void If set to true the curret property is hidden from its parent instance. <property object>.getDatatype() => string Returns the datatype of the current property. Please see Specification > Properties > datatype documentation for more information about Data Types. <property object>.setDatatype(datatype: string) => void Sets the datatype of the current property. It is largely NOT RECOMMENDED to change the datatype of a property outside of setting the property in the properties.yaml file. Please see Specification > Properties > datatyle documentation for more information about Data Types. <property object>.getKey() => void Returns the key of the current property. Please note that the key of a property is read-only and cannot be changed. <property object>.getName() => string Returns the name of the current property. <property object>.setName(name: string) => void Sets the name of the current property. <property object>.getDescription() => string Returns the description of the current property. <property object>.setDescription(description: string) => void Sets the description of the current property. <property object>.getDocumentation() => string Returns the documetation of the current property. <property object>.setDocumentation(documentation: string) => void Sets the documentation of the current property. <property object>.getDefault() => unknown Returns the default value of the current property. <property object>.setDefault(value: unknown) => void Sets the default value of the current property. <property object>.getGroup() => string Returns the group of the current property. Please see Specification > Properties > group for more information about Groups. <property object>.setGroup(group: string) => void Sets the group of the current property. Please see Specification > Properties > group for more information about Groups. <property object>.getRequired() => boolean Returns the required flag of the current property. <property object>.setRequired(required: boolean) => void Sets the required flag of the current property. <property object>.getPersist() => boolean Returns the presist flag of the current property. <property object>.setPersist(persist: boolean) => void Sets the persist flag of the current property. <property object>.getOrder() => number Returns the order position number of the current property. Please see Specification > Properties > order for more information about Ordering. <property object>.setOrder(order: number) => void Sets the order position number of the current property. Please see Specification > Properties > order for more information about Ordering. <property object>.getReadOnly() => boolean Returns the read-only flag of the current property. <property object>.setReadOnly(readonly: boolean) => void Sets the read-only flag of the current property. Examples​ const count = context.getProperty('count'); count.datatype; // get datatype count.set('datatype', 'text'); count.hidden; // get hidden field count.set('hidden', true); count.get(); // get data on the property count.set('data', 'hello'); count.remove(); // remove property, only if property is dynamic count.hide(); // hide property

searchDocs.title: generate
searchDocs.content: Experimental generate What is Module Generation?​ Generate is a powerful way to create modules with minimal work. For example, one can generate an API Node if an URL or OpenAPI specification is given. Generated modules typically comes with a lot of common features that the end-user may need (e.g. an API module comes with debounce configuration out-of-the-box). Benefits​ Consistent user-experience.No need to reinvent the wheel.Batteries included.Can still add custom code logic and override generated properties.Works in any supported language. When to use Generate?​ An API request based module that fetches data via rest API endpoints.An embed module that inserts a view of an external website into a module.An extended module that derives from a parent module. Custom Overrides​ When generate is used, a Node can still have custom logic/code. The code will be compiled together with the generated module. By default, the Node's code is appended after the generated code, thus allowing the Node's code to modify the generated code. If it is required to execute some code before the generated code, configuration allows specific code to be prepended before the generated code. Types of Generated Modules​ There are three types of generated modules, each with thier own usage and configuration. request A request generated module is a clean and standard approach to requesting data from some external resource. You provide the URL or OpenAPI specification and any supporting information (like security tokens, pagination details, etc), and Request will go get you the data in the most performant way. Request comes in two flavors: URL or OpenAPI. URL: Using the URL form of Request, the system will fetch data from the given URL and provided parameters and configuration.OpenAPI: Given an OpenAPI Specification, Request will fetch data from the OpenAPI endpoint and provide parameters and configuration using the OpenAPI specification. Please read the (Documentation for request Generation) for more information. embed An embed generated module is a way to insert the view of an external website into your module. It does this by wrapping the request for the website within a <iframe> HTML tag, thus isolating that view. For example, you might want to inject a certain YouTube video into your module. Please read the (Documentation for embed generation) for more information. extends An extends generate module is one that derives itself from a parent module, the module from which you are extending. The Node you are currently building will have all of the configuration and properties of the module from which you extend. You can then change and overload those properties to further differentiate your module from the module extended. An example of this might might be an Email Text Input field, which extends from the generic Text Input field, but differ in that it only excepts email addresses. Please read the (Documentation for extends generation) for more information.

searchDocs.title: Imports
searchDocs.content: Imports A module may import a variety of both relative and external code or packages. Largely importing adheres to standard JavaScript/TypeScript rules, but there a few special edge cases one should be aware of depending upon the style of import and what is being imported. Standard Imports​ JavaScript/Typescript both support standard imports via thier import keyword. These can be relative code (eg, ./MyOtherCode.js) or external packages (eg. express). Relative Imports​ A relative import refers to any file located within your module development space. A relative import always starts with either ./ or ../. Please note it is not possible to import something below the root of your project. For example, if given the following tree structure... ./ manifest.yaml properties.yaml src/ main.js module1/ MyModule1.js module2/ MyModule2.js The following imports would work: From src/main.js: import Module1 from './module1/MyModule1'; import Module2 from './module2/MyModule2'; from src/module1/MyModule1.js: import Module2 from '../module2/MyModule2'; from src/module2/MyModule2.js: import Module1 from '../module1/MyModule1'; External Imports​ Any NPM package can also be imported using the import JavaScript/TypeScript keyword. import uuid from 'uuid'. When an import occurs, Openexus parses the module code and pulls any NPM package imports out, inserts them into a package.json file, then builds all the code using that package.json file. If a package.json already exists and the module is reference there already, the insertion is skipped; otherwise, the module is inserted into the existing package.json. Versioning​ It is possible to target a specific version for importing by specifying it in a package.json file. This package.json file must be at the root of your module, alongside your manifest and properties files. Because this is just a package.json file, it follows the standard npm versioning scheme for specifying a version based on Semantic Versionion semantics. Dynamic Imports​ Dynamic Importing is supported in both JavaScript and Typescript using the import() function. Using dynamic imports mostly follows the same rules as using a Standard Import with the following differences: The import() function returns a promise that must be awaited in order to use it.When specifying a relative import you MUST specify the extension of the relative import. Make sure to add the .js or .ts or whatever extension, such that it is a full path to the file.The import() function has different output than the import keyword, because one is a keyword and the other a function. In this case, the function version outputs an object that represents the exported object from the exported package/file. Obtaining the default export requires referncing the .default property of the imported object. Obtaining other exported things is done by name. ./src/MyModule.js export function myFunction() { ... }; export default function myDefaultFunction() { ... }; ./src/main.js const importedMyModule = await import('./myModule.js') const myDefaultFunc = importedMyModule.default; const myFunc = importedModule.myFunction; Relative Imports​ A relative import refers to any file located within your module development space. A relative import always starts with either ./ or ../. Please note it is not possible to import something below the root of your project. NOTE: When importing dynamically via the import() function, you must specify the full path to the module including its extension. For example, if given the following tree structure... ./ manifest.yaml properties.yaml src/ main.js module1/ MyModule1.js module2/ MyModule2.js The following imports would work: From src/main.js: import('./module1/MyModule1'); import('./module2/MyModule2'); from 'src/module1/MyModule1.js': import('../module2/MyModule2'); from src/module2/MyModule2.js: import('../module1/MyModule1'); External Imports​ Any NPM package can also be imported using the import() function. import('uuid'); When an import occurs, Openexus parses the module code and pulls any NPM package imports out, inserts them into a package.json file, then builds all the code using that package.json file. If a package.json already exists and the module is reference there already, the insertion is skipped; otherwise, the module is inserted into the existing package.json. Versioning​ It is possible to target a specific version for importing by specifying it in a package.json file. This package.json file must be at the root of your module, alongside your manifest and properties files. Because this is just a package.json file, it follows the standard npm versioning scheme for specifying a version based on Semantic Versionion semantics. Examples​ import chartjs from 'chartjs/auto'; Importing UMD Javascript/Typescript packages​

searchDocs.title: Asset Configuration
searchDocs.content: Asset Configuration An Asset within the Openexus Node Specification is any file included as part of the Node specification that is not source code. These could be images, audio files, video files, HTML files, CSS files, text files, data file, or literally anything else. Supported Asset Types​ Technically, any file in your Node's specification is an asset and can be reference thus. However, not all things can read or use an asset file of a given type and thus whether or not a given asset works with a given thing is entirely dependent on the thing using it. Largely speaking the following should be true for supported assets: Images: .jpeg, .gif, .pngAudio: .wav, .au, .mp3Video: .mp4, .ogv, webmHTML: .htm, .html, .xhtml, .cssText: .txt, .textDocs: .pdf, .doc, .docx MIME Types and Asset Files​ Assets are served with a MIME Type that is guessed by its file extension. There is no way to override the MIME Type of a given asset at this time. The following file extensions are recognized and mapped to the given MIME Type. .gif - image/gif.jpg - image/jpeg.jpeg - image/jpeg.png - image/png.txt - text/plain.text - text/plain.htm - text/html.html - text/html.xhtml - text/html.csv - text/csv.css - text/css.wav - audio/vnd.wav.mp3 - audio/mpeg.mp4 - video/mp4.ogv - video/ogg.webm - video/webm.pdf - application/pdf.doc - application/msword Referencing Asset Files​ While building your node and source code it will become necessary at some point to reference a specific asset. This is done by relatively referencing the needed file. For example, if there is the following node structure: Number Double Node - manifest.yaml - properties.yaml - src - main.js - assets - screenshot.png And you want to reference the screenshot.png from manifest.yaml the reference would be ./assets/screenshot.png. The manifest.yaml file is always at the root of the node and nothing below it exists nor is exposed via reference.

searchDocs.title: Code Configuration
searchDocs.content: Code Configuration The Source Code of a Module is any part of the Module's specification that contains executable software instructions in the form of a supported programming language. When a Module is used the source code is interpretted and run to produce the Module's output. Additionally, as the Module is interacted with, the source code can respond to the changes in the Module and produce different output. Some Modules require no source code while other require a little source and still others require lots of source code. It all depends on what the objective of the Module is. Supported Languages​ Currently Openexus supports the following languages for source code: JavaScriptTypeScript Frameworks​ In addition to supported languages, some languages also have specific frameworks that work with Openexus. For example, you can write your Module's Source Code in JavaScript using the React framework. This means that the Source Code supports the language and framework you are most comfortable using. Using a Framework is mostly only useful when creating a Module that has a UI component to it and takes advantage of these UI frameworks. Currently the following frameworks are supported within the following languages: JavaScript & TypeScript Standard (aka Vanilla) / No FrameworkSolidReactVueSvelte Openexus SDK​ In order to interact and work within Openexus your Source Code will need to use the Openexus SDK. The SDK defines a series of Types, Objects, Functions, etc, as appropriate to the language of choice, that are used to manipulate the Module and its surrounding instances. The SDK is its own section of this documentation and further broken down by language of choice. Please visit the SDK sections below to learn more about all the SDK calls. JavaScript and TypeScript SDK Whenever possible Openexus has attempted to make the SDK as similar as possible across languages; however, this is not always entirely feasible and differences and nuances may exist between them.
