searchDocs.title: Introduction
searchDocs.content: Introduction The Openexus Module Specification defines the structure and details to describe a Module and all of its supporting code and assets. When a Module is used, the Openexus Module Specification is interpretted to produce the Module and execute the code. There are three (3) major components to the specification: a Manifest declaration;a Properties declaration;and Source Code. Each of these components is described below and in the following sections. Manifest​ The manifest declaration describes the metadata of the Module and all additional configuration for it. This include the name of the Module, a description of it, an icon for it, and all supporting configuration. It should be noted, that the properties of a Module are described outside of this file, but everything else is configured within the manifest. A manifest is required for every Module. A very simple manifest may have these fields: manifest.yaml name: Number Doubler description: Simple module that doubles a number. icon: mdi:star Read more information about the contents of manifest declaration. Properties​ The properties declaration describes the specific properties of a Module. A Module may have zero or more properties and each property is configured in this properties declaration. properties.yaml value: description: Provide the number to double. datatype: number default: 1 double: description: The doubled value. datatype: number default: 2 Read more information about the contents of properties declaration. Source Code​ The source code of a Module consists of zero or more source files in the progreamming language specified in the manifest. Source code is not always required, but any kind of logic or special behavior of a Module will most certainly need it. Source code may have any structure desired, but it is strongly recommended that it be placed under a folder named /src. The default source code entry point is src/main.js and it is recommended that all code begin there. src/main.js context.subscribe('value', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); Read more information about the source code. searchDocs.title: Utils Components [deprecated]
searchDocs.content: Utils Components [deprecated] Common utils components are provided and imported from @modules-js/components. For​ The <For> component is used to render a list of items. It is similar to the .map() function in JavaScript. <For each={context.get("data")} fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}> {(item) => <div>{item}</div>} </For> The optional second argument is an index signal. <For each={context.get("data")} fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}> {(item, index) => ( <div> #{index()} {item} </div> )} </For> Show​ The Show control flow is used to conditional render part of the view: it renders children when the when is truthy, a fallback otherwise. It is similar to the ternary operator (when ? children : fallback) but is ideal for templating JSX. <Show when={context.get("count") > 0} fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}> <div>My Content</div> </Show> Switch / Match​ Useful for when there are more than 2 mutual exclusive conditions. It is a more flexible version of the if-else-if-else-if-else-... chain. <Switch fallback={<div>Not Found</div>}> <Match when={state.route === "home"}> <Home /> </Match> <Match when={state.route === "settings"}> <Settings /> </Match> </Switch> Index​ Non-keyed list iteration (rendered nodes are keyed to an array index). This is useful when there is no conceptual key, like if the data consists of primitives and it is the index that is fixed rather than the value. Usage is the same as <For>. <Index each={context.get("data")} fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}> {(item, index) => ( <div> #{index} {item()} </div> )} </Index>

searchDocs.title: direction
searchDocs.content: direction Properties by default are reactive and bi-directional, meaning they are both read and write. However, indicating how the Property is used can be very useful for the user to understand the intent of the properties. The direction Property field can be used to do this. If a Property is only read and never written (e.g. only context.get('query') and not context.set("query", newValue)), it would be an input property. If a Property is written (e.g. only context.get('result') and not context.set("result", newValue)), it would be an output property. If a Property is both read and written in a reactively way (e.g. both context.get('value') and context.set("value", newValue) are used in the module), the direction would be both. direction values​ both: This Property can be both read (get) or written (set).output: This Property can only be read (get).input: This Property can only be written (set). Example​ properties.yaml query: datatype: text direction: input result: datatype: json direction: output value: datatype: json direction: both

searchDocs.title: Manifest Declaration
searchDocs.content: Manifest Declaration Each Module requires a Manifest declaration. In the Manifest declaration you define the Module configuration as described in the Manifest Fields below. A manifest must include, at a minimum, the following fields: name and description, but may also include any of the optional fields like icon or keywords. manifest.yaml name: Number Doubler description: Simple module that doubles a number. icon: mdi:star Manifest Fields​ name - Visible title for the Module, displayed to whenever the design view of a Module is shownin Openexus. description - A description about what the node does. The description of the Module should be relatively short. To add more details beyond the description, use the documentation field. icon - A reference to one of Openexus exposed public icons which can be found here: https://icon-sets.iconify.design. documentation - Longer form details about how the Module works and anything a module developer using the Module would need to know or do. categories - Categorical tags for the Module used when organizaing Modules for user selection. You may specify up to two categories in a comma separated format from the following category list. Any category that does not meet this list or exceeds the category allowance will be ignored. Please see the Categories section below. keywords - Useful keywords that this Module may be found under when searching for new Modules. You may specify any number of keywords as a comma-separated string. Keywords are case-insensitive and may contain spaces, but may not start with or end with a space. thumbnail - A thumbnail image to represent this Module. A thumbnail must be a fully formed url to an image externally available. screenshots - Zero or more screenshots to illustrate this Module and how it works. Screenshots must be a fully formed url to an image externally available. Examples​ Some examples of manifest declarations. A Simple Input Field Example​ name: Input description: Input field for user input purpose: Input field to accept user input. Great for entering text, numbers, url, emails, etc. Useful to bind with other modules that require user input. instructions: icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png name: Button description: A simple button that can trigger actions purpose: Input field to accept user input. Great for entering text, numbers, url, emails, etc. Useful to bind with other modules that require user input. instructions: icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png A Button Example​ name: API Fetch description: A simple button that can trigger actions purpose: Input field to accept user input. Great for entering text, numbers, url, emails, etc. Useful to bind with other modules that require user input. instructions: icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png A Fetch Example​ name: Unit Conversion description: A conversion node that can convert between two values. Types of conversion includes time, length, data, volume, area, mass, temperature, power, angle, and more. purpose: Great for instructions: ... icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png A Unit Conversion Example​

searchDocs.title: persist
searchDocs.content: persist Experimental Persist allows you to configure whether the data for this property is persisted across reloads. If true any value set to this property will be stored for any usage, if possible, and persist across usage/reloads. If not set to true, any value set will not persist across usage/reloads. persist value​ true: If true, any value set on the property will automatically persist across reloads, if possible.false: If false, any value set on the property WILL NO persist across reloads. persist storage​ If a user is logged in, persisted values are written to the Openexus data storage and availabe any time the user reloads. This allows for persisted values across browsers and devices. If a user is not logged in, persisted values are written to the Browsers localStorage feature and avauilable any time the user reloads within the same browser. Cross browser and cross device persistance is not available when a user is not logged into openexus.

searchDocs.title: group
searchDocs.content: group Use the group Property field to group a Module's related properties together. When a Module is displayed to a user, grouped properties are called out into their own area which contains each Property of the group. The group value is purely for display purposes and has no impact on any other aspect of using a Property. group field​ The group Property field can contain any string you want, but it is desirable to keep this short (less than 16 characters or so) and minmize any non-alphanumeric characters. group ordering​ When a Module has groups the are renderer in the order they first occur within the Properties Declaration. For example, if we had the below properties with groups defined the order of the groups would be Visualization followed by Options. properties.yaml value: datatype: text show_value: datatype: boolean group: Visualization min: datatype: number group: Options max: datatype: number group: Options Example​ properties.yaml value: datatype: text min: datatype: number group: Options max: datatype: number group: Options show_value: datatype: boolean group: Options

searchDocs.title: order
searchDocs.content: order Modules can have a lot of properties. The order Property field can be used to indicate the importance of the Property. Larger order numbers are more important and thus have better visibility. Negative numbers are automatically collapsed and initialliy hidden. The order number you set is a hint on where a Property should be displayed relative to the other properties. order value​ The order Property field takes a number. The number you give order determines how important the Property is when displayed. Higher positive numbers are displayed higher up and thus more visible.Lower positive numbers are displayed lower down and this less visible.zero is treated as a lower positive number.Negative numbers are collapsed in the display and hidden behind the "More..." toggle. NOTE: order is entirely about how properties are displayed and has no impact on the property itself. NOTE: If a property has a group then the order of properties within that group is what we are defining with the order property. Where a group is displayed is not impacted by order or properties with an order property. That is to say, if we have both group and order on a property, the order value is only relevant within the group and not within the greater hierarchy of properties. Example​ properties.yaml value: datatype: text order: 10 # Most prominent because it has the highest order min: datatype: number order: -1 # Collapsed by default because negative max: datatype: number order: -1 # Collapsed by default because negative label: datatype: text # Default order of 0

searchDocs.content: Setup Experimental Setup allows a Node to quickly setup the other nodes in relation to the node being created. Essentilly, it allows a Node to be built of other nodes, connections, bindings and data. Setup is a powerful way to have nested relationship. manifest.yaml name: See Characters in Text! setup: modules: input: input/number/number_input slider: input/number/slider_input text_util: utilities/text/text_analyze connections: - input/value <=> text_util/value - slider/value <=> text_util/characters bindings: - this/ui = input/ui - this/ui2 = slider/ui data: - input/value = "test" Setup Configuration​ Setup descrbes modules, connections, bindings, and data and how theses things relate to the current node. modules​ Modules are each specified thus: [local-name]: [module identifier][version] local-name is a name for this module that is local to the node and only used for purposes of this setup configuration. module-identifier is a full reference to the module to add, of the form @username/moduleKey. version may optionally be appended to the module-identifier if the specific version is known and desired, for example openexus/TextInput@v1.0.7. manifest.yaml setup: modules: input: input/number/number_input slider: input/number/slider_input text_util: utilities/text/text_analyze In the above example this adds three modules with the local names of input, slider and text_util. connections​ Using the local names of the modules setup in the prior step, connections can be made between those modues and/or this node. We specify the connection as so: [local-name/port-key] [direction] [local-name/port-key] [port-key] [direction] [local-name.port-key] [local-name/port-key] [direction] [port-key] local-name is the name of the module as defined in the prior section. If local-name is omitted, the port-key is on the current node, not a module included above. port-key is a port key as specified in a node/module's properties file. direction specifies the connection direction and how data flows between the two ports. It may be one of the following: <=> - flow is bi-directional and travels both ways.=> - flow is one-way and travels from the module/node on the left to the module/node on the right.=> - flow is one-way and travels from the module/node on the right to the module/node on the left. manifest.yaml name: See Characters in Text! setup: connections: - input/value <=> text_util/value - slider/value <=> text_util/characters bindings​ TODO: What are bindings? data​ Using a local-name and port-key, assign a specific value to the port. The value must be valid according to the port's datatype. [local-name/port-key] = [value] [port-key] = [value] local-name is the name of the module as defined in the prior section. If local-name is omitted, the port-key is on the current node, not a module included above. port-key is a port key as specified in a node/module's properties file.

searchDocs.title: datatype
searchDocs.content: datatype The datatype Property field provides a hint to Openexus and users as to what kind of thing a Property can hold. This in turn steers what a Property can connect to and interact with. Data Types are useful indicators on how properties can communicate with other properties. Here's just a small example smattering of Data Type usage... properties.yaml ui: Data Type: html slot: Data Type: '[html]' some_datatype_I_have: Data Type: text some_action: Data Type: action properties: - key: id Data Type: text some_trigger: Data Type: trigger your_secret: Data Type: secret Types​ Primitive Data Types​ Standard primitive Data Types are simple, fundamental structures. text - Holds text like "Openexus is great!". This is sometimes called a "string" in other programming languages and systems. boolean - A type that can be either true or false, nothing else. number - Holds a number value, be it a whole numer or a real number. Dates​ Support for working with Dates and Times. Please also see js-date - Holds the date in a JavaScript Date() object. Compound Data Types​ Compound types are types that are a compond of other types. Examples include arrays, object, json, maps, dictionaries, and lists. [_type_] - Array of a certain type (remember to replace _type_ with one of the primitives) For example: [boolean] which can hold values like: [ true , false , true ] json - Holds a JavaScript object For example: json => { a : 1, b : 2 }. json-text - Holds a JavaScript object in string format => "{a:1,b:2}". option - Holds a list of options you specify. You have to list the options with the Data Type as well. For example: position: Data Type: type: option options: - top - bottom UI & Slot Data Types​ Specific to the rendering of a Module, these types indiciate that the Property will have a function that will return HTML. html - Holds the rendered output of a Module. This means when used, the HTML of the Module will be returned for that Module. [html] - Holds a slot input into a Module, which is an array of html. Usually used to join up other html types together into a layout. Trigger Data Type​ trigger - A trigger Data Type is a special type that is used to notify of some event on a Module. When an event is fired or emitted from the Module, any connection to the associated trigger will be notified. For example, a button Module may have a on_click property with datatype: trigger. trigger properties can only connect to action properties. Action Data Type​ action - An action Data Type is a special type that is used to execute or run some behavior of the Module. When an action receives notification from a trigger, the associated behavior is executed. For example, on_click (trigger) can be connected to a send_email (action). It may be helpful to think of an action as a function or block of code that can execute when a trigger connected to it has an event. action properties can only connect to trigger properties. Any Data Type​ The any Data Type means that a Property can accept connections from any other Data Type. Largely, one should avoid using any as a Data Type as it will make connections harder to use. Extended Data Types​ Extended Data Types are Data Types which derive themselves from a more common parent type, such as the types above. As such, they can connect to properties with the parent type in addition to those of the same type. For example, a email type can connect to another email type or to it's parent type of text. Note: Some Extended Data Types may be validated to make sure they conform to their specific type needs and setting a value on these properties may throw errors if they fail validation. For example, an email type is validated to ensure that it meets Email Address formatting. Extends text​ The following types all extend the text Data Type and thus can connect to properties of the same type or properties of type text. For example, a email type can connect to another email type or to it's parent type of text. Extends text (Identity)​ email - Holds an email in plain text. Validated to check if it is in email format (has an @ sign). name - Holds a person's full name in plain text. first-name - Holds a person's first name in plain text. last-name - Holds a person's last name in plain text. username - Holds a username in plain text. password - Holds a password in plain text. Extends text (Secrets)​ secret - Holds a reference to a secret value that cannot be displayed, only used. Usually for API keys or holding sensitive passwords. A secret type is intentionally obscured from users and developers to protect their contents and avoid exposing this information. The secret is only fetched when it is needed in a module. Extends text (Currency)​ currency - Holds a number and a currency. currency-alpha - Holds the currency in plain text as a 3 letter currency code (ISO 4217). For example: USD, EUR, JPY cc-number - Holds a Credit Card number in plain text. Validated to check that the value matches known Credit Card Number standards. Same as credit-card-number below. credit-card-number - Holds a Credit Card number in plain text. Validated to check that the value matches known Credit Card Number standards. Same as cc-number above. Extends text (Technical)​ url - Holds a URL in plain text. Validated to check if it is in URL format (starts with http:// or https://). uuid - Holds a Universally Unique Identifier in plain text. Validated to check if it is in uuid format (36 alphanumeric with dashes). ip - Holds an Internet Protocol address in plain text. This may be either an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Validated to check if it is in an IPv4 or IPv6 address format. ipv4 - Holds an Internet Protocol address in plain text. This must be an IPv4 address. Validated to check if it is in an IPv4 address format. ipv6 - Holds an Internet Protocol address in plain text. This must be an IPv6 address. Validated to check if it is in an IPv6 address format. sql-statement - Holds an sql statement in plain text. jmes-path - Holds a jmes-path in plain text. css-stylesheet - Holds a css-stylesheet in plain text. css-unit - Holds a css-unit in plain text. For example: 12px, 1rem, 2em, etc Extends text (Colors)​ css-color - Holds a css color in plain text. These may be of any supported CSS color expression form. Please see MDN <color> value documenation for more details. color-css - Holds a password in plain text. These may be of any supported CSS color expression form. Please see MDN <color> value documenation for more details. color-hex - Holds a color represented as a hexadecimal string. color-rgb - Holds an color represented as a RGB string of three decimal octets. Extends text (Location)​ location - Holds a latitude and a longitude pair. In the format of ISO 6709 (/ is terminating, no comma). For example: "+48.8577+002.295/" country - Holds a country name in full. For example: "United States of America" country-alpha-2 - Holds a two letter country code in plain text. For example: US, CN, IN country-alpha-3 - Holds a two letter country code. For example: USA, CHN, IND timezone - Holds the timezone specified in a string. Extends text (Date and Time)​ datetime - Holds the Date and Time in plain text. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (UTC). date - Holds a Date in plain text. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-MM-DD. time - Holds a Time in plain text. In the format of ISO 8601: hh:mm:ss. timezone - Holds the timezone specified in a string. In the format of ISO-8601 Time Zone. For example: +04:00 year-week - Holds a date in plain text with the year and week. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-Wxx. For example: 2024-W18 year-week-day - Holds a date in plain text with the year, week and day. ISO 8601: YYYY-W1xx-x. For example: 2024-W18-4 year-ordinal-date - Holds a date in plain text with the year, ordinal and day. ISO 8601: YYYY-ddd. For example: 2024-123 year-month - Holds a date in plain text with the year and month. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-MM. Extends number​ The following type all extend the number Data Type and thus can connect to properties of the same type or properties of type number. Extends number (Currency)​ currency-numeric - Holds the currency as a 3 digit number currency code (ISO 4217). For example: 840, 978, 392 Extends number (Location)​ country-code-numeric - Holds a number referring to a country. E.g 840, 156, 356 zipcode-us - Holds a US zipcode in as a number. For example: 94043 Extends number (Date and Time)​ datetime-epoch - Holds the datetime (Unix Epoch/POSIX time) in plain text as a number. For example: 1618921342 Other Data Types​ The following additional Data Types are also supported. pointer-event - Holds the pointer event of a mouse/touch event. data - Holds general data from an API response. image - Holds an image in the form of a blob string. file - Holds a file in the form of a blob or URL reference. Default Type​ If no datatype is specified for a Property, the default type of any is used. As we mention above, it is undesireable to use the any type, so please avoid not providing a datatype for properties. Datatypes & Connections​ Datatypes provide a useful hint as to how Modules can communicate with each other, similar to typing in a programming language. Some common rules are: any can always connect with any other Property, irregardless of Data Type.trigger Data Types can only be connected with action Data Types. Platforms that implement the spec can decide how to treat connections with different Data Types. On openexus, when different Data Types are connected (For example: number to text), we will provide a warning to the user and also try our best to cast the Data Types accordingly. Data Type Coercion​ When you connect two properties together of differing Data Types, Openexus will attempt to coerce one Data Type into another as apprpriate. The following shows how that coercion works: Source Value	Target Type	Target Value	Coerced	Notesundefined	undefined	undefined	No undefined	null	null	Yes undefined	boolean	false	Yes undefined	number	0	Yes undefined	string	''	Yes undefined	Date	undefined	No null	undefined	undefined	Yes null	null	null	No null	boolean	false	Yes null	number	0	Yes null	string	''	Yes null	Date	null	No true	undefined	undefined	Yes true	null	null	Yes true	boolean	true	No true	number	1	Yes true	string	'true'	Yes true	Date	undefined	Yes false	undefined	undefined	Yes false	null	null	Yes false	boolean	false	No false	number	0	Yes false	string	'false'	Yes false	Date	undefined	Yes 0	undefined	undefined	Yes 0	null	null	Yes 0	boolean	false	Yes 0	number	0	No 0	string	'0'	Yes 0	Date	1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z	Yes 1 (not zero)	undefined	undefined	Yes 1 (not zero)	null	null	Yes 1 (not zero)	boolean	true	Yes 1 (not zero)	number	1	No 1 (not zero)	string	'1'	Yes 1 (not zero)	Date	1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z	Yes '' (String)	undefined	undefined	Yes '' (String)	null	null	Yes '' (String)	boolean	false	Yes '' (String)	number	0	Yes	1 '' (String)	string	''	No '' (String)	Date	undefined	Yes	2 'abc' (String)	undefined	undefined	Yes 'abc' (String)	null	null	Yes 'abc' (String)	boolean	true	Yes 'abc' (String)	number	0	Yes	1 'abc' (String)	string	'abc'	No 'abc' (String)	Date	undefined	Yes	2 Notes: 1: Strings coerced into numbers will attempted to read the string as a radix 10 number according to JavaScript coercion rules. Any non-numeric characters ([0-9], [-], [e], and [.]) will be stripped out and then the number will be coerced, if possible.2: Strings coerced into Dates will attempted to be parsed as dates, but if not possilbe will return undefined. The Big Data Type Table​ You can see all the Data Types in one big table here, if that is easier to work with: Data Types table

searchDocs.title: Properties Declaration
searchDocs.content: Properties Declaration The Properties declaration describes a Module's data points, the input and output of a Module. When a Module receives input from another Module it comes across one of these properties. When a Module produces output of any type, it sends that output by way of one of these properties. Properties consist of a property key and zero or more optional configuration details. properties.yaml value: description: Provide a number, and get back the double value in ((double)). datatype: number default: 1 order: 20 double: description: The doubled value. order: 10 readonly: true Property Keys​ Each Property needs to have a unique key. This is the key that will be used for referencing this Property and performing value lookups against it. Requirements for a key are as follows: Keys are case sensitive.A key must start with alpha character of the form [A-Z] or [a-z].A key may have an alpha character of the form [A-Z] or [a-z].A key may have a numeric character of the form [0-9], but it may not be the first character.A key may have an underscore character, but it may not be the first character. Once a Module is published and in-use by others, changing the key may affect existing connections. Property Data Type​ A Property Data Type is an additional configuration point for a Property. The Data Type of a Property describes what type of values of data that Property can hold. This is used when two Modules are connected together. Connections are only possible if they Data Type of the two Properties being connected are aligned. If a property is missing a Data Type, the default Data Type is applied and used. The Data Type of a property is specified by the datatype field of the property configuration. Possible Data Types are described in the datatype property documentation. It is strongly recommended that a Data Type be included for each Property. Do not rely on the default Data Type. It is very loose and will not combine with other types well. Property Fields​ datatype: The type of data this field holds. Possible values are described in the datatype property documentation.default: the default value of the property field.description: A short, human readable description of the property field.direction: The directionality of the property field. Possible values are described in the direction property documenation.documentation: Longer form documentation for the property field, if needed. group: A logical grouping for propeties. A property that is given a group will be visually grouped together with properties of the same group when visually displayed. If no group is given, the properties are not grouped. More details can be found in the group property documenation.hidden: If true this property is hidden and not shown when the Module is displayed visually.name: The name or label of this property. Has a maximum of 256 characters. If a name is not provided, Openexus will use the key and attempt to format it nicely. This may not always be quite correct, so feel free to use the name field to override that behavior.order: The importance of the property; a higher number indicates more importance. More details can be found in the order property documenation. required: If true this property is required to have a value. value: The value of the property field. This differs from the default in that the default is used ONLY IF the value is not set. Examples​ Some examples of Property Declarations. ui: datatype: html data: purpose: Incoming data to display on a table. Commonly connected to the [result] property of api modules so that we can show data. Array of objects are required to show in a table. If an object instead of an array is provided instead, this module can best guess the array to display in the table. If the guess is incorrect, [data_query] property can be used to transform the data to an array. datatype: json order: 10 data_query: description: Transform the data using JMESPath (https://jmespath.org). purpose: "Transform the data using JMESPath (https://jmespath.org). You can use common dot notion to transverse the data object. For example, given an object { list: [1,2,3] }, setting [data_query] as '.list' will return just the array [1,2,3]. If the intention is to selective only show some columns, use the [columns] property, do not need to use the [data_query] property." datatype: json order: 10 table_columns: name: Columns description: Columns to show. purpose: Define the columns to show in the table. Update this property if we want to selectively only show some columns from the given data. If not provided, all columns would be shown. Update this property with a comma seperated string. For example, "id,name,rating" will only show the id, name, and rating keys from the given object. datatype: text order: 10 selected_row: description: Data for the selected row. purpose: Get the data for the selected row. This can be useful to connect the selected data to show additional details. datatype: any selected_row_index: description: Selected row index. datatype: number result: purpose: Result of the NASA Earth Imagery which returns a satelite image of a specified point and dimension on earth. order: 10 datatype: image api_key: datatype: text default: niceTry hidden: true lat: description: Latitude of the satelite image to get datatype: text required: true lon: description: Longitude of the satelite image to get datatype: text required: true dim: description: Dimension of the image in degrees datatype: text default: 0.025 date: description: Date to fetch in YYYY-MM-DD datatype: text required: true default: "2024-05-01"

searchDocs.title: Slots
searchDocs.content: Slots A Module can be used to render other Modules, usually providing a specific type of layout for those child Modules. This is accomplied by using a property we call a slot. A slot is a specific property setup to connect with other Modules rendering. A slot property looks like this: properties.yaml slot: datatype: '[html]' Because a slot is rendering out other Modules UI properties, we should probably also have a UI property along with our slot to display the output. Like this... properties.yaml ui: datatype: html slot: datatype: '[html]' Now that we have our properties setup, there remains but one thing to do: render our slot input to our ui output. The manner we do this is slightly different for each framework, but substantively its the same idea; render each UI connected to your slot in some order, applying some set of layout or otherwise as we go. The best way to demonstrate this is to show you how we do it. VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid This is a very basic example to illustrate the concept of a slot. Consider using a templating engine like pug, hyperscript, lit or a frontend framework. src/main.js function render(element) { // Since ((slot)) has the datatype [html], an array of render functions will be returned const slot = context.get('slot') || []; // Loop through each item and call the function provided slot.forEach((uiRender) => { const uiElement = document.createElement('div'); element.appendChild(uiElement); // Pass in the element for the render function to mount uiRender?.(uiEl); }); } context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.title: UI & Rendering
searchDocs.content: UI & Rendering Some Modules may want to render output to the screen. In order to do this, the Module must expose a Property to render this content. We call these Properties "UI properties". NOTE: Not all Modules will have a UI Property. Only Modules that have a visual component to them should have a UI Property. If a Module does not have a visual component to it, it does not need to have a UI Property. Creating UI Properties​ To create a UI Property, create a Property in your Property declaration that has a Data Type of html. This indicates to Openexus that the output of this property is a render function. A render function is a function which takes a parent element and produces a rendered result. This result may be to either mutate the parent element, or to produce a block of HTML content to insert. Here's an example of creating a UI Property: properties.yaml ui: datatype: html NOTE: A UI Property does not have to use the proeprty key ui. Other keys can be used. However, using ui is a standard approach in Openexus and encouraged. Rendering​ A render function is a JavaScript/TypeScript function that gets called when any part of the Instance changes. These changes trigger rendering and the render function gets called to produce the new output. The render function is called with the following signature: (parentElement: HTMLElement) => string The parentElement argument is a reference to the element in which the result of the render function will be rendered. For some frameworks this is required, for others it is not. The returned string from the render function is any valid HTML content including HTML Tags. This content is directly inserted into the parentElement to produce the final view of the module instance. Setting a UI Property​ A UI Property is just a Property that takes as a value the render function. It is critical to make sure to set your UI Property to the function being used to render, as shown here in this code: properties.yaml ui: datatype: html src/main.js function render() { return `<p>Hello there!</p>`; } context.set('ui', render) In the above the function named render is set as the value of the ui Property. Working with Frameworks​ Each framework will have its own approach to rendering. These might include creating elements or using JSX/TSX. Because each framework is different, they may have slight differences how the render function works. Please consult our extensive Framework documentation to learn more details. Example​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid Simple counter button example without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: Counter description: Simple counter example. properties.yaml ui: datatype: html count: datatype: number default: 1 src/main.js let button; function render(element) { button = document.createElement('button'); button.innerHTML = `Count is ${context.get('count')}`; button.addEventListener('click', (value) => { context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); }); element.appendChild(button); } // Subscribe to ((count)) changes context.subscribe('count', (value) => { if (button) button.innerHTML = `Count is ${value}`; }); // Set the ((ui)) property to be the render function context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.title: generate > request
searchDocs.content: Experimental generate > request A request generated module is a clean and standard approach to requesting data from some external resource. We provide the URL or an OpenAPI specification and any supporting information (like security tokens, pagination details, etc), and Request will go get the data in the most performant way. Request comes in two flavors: URL or OpenAPI. URL: Using the URL form of Request, the system will fetch data from the given URL and provided parameters and configuration.OpenAPI: Given an OpenAPI Specification, Request will fetch data from the OpenAPI endpoint and provide parameters and configuration using the OpenAPI specification. URL Requests​ The URL form of request takes some URL and some parameters and fetches data from that URL. Using this method creates a more robust form of requesting that data rather than just directly issuing the fetch call in the code. manifest.yaml name: 'Pokémon', description: 'Pokémon are the creatures that inhabit the world of the Pokémon games. They can be caught using Pokéballs and trained by battling with other Pokémon. This module returns the abilities and various stats of pokemons.', icon: 'ic:baseline-catching-pokemon', generate: { type: 'fetch', config: { url: `https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/pokemon/((pokemon))`, params: 'offset,limit', }, }, URL Request Configuration​ type: This must be set to fetch. config: The request configuration. See below for specific URL request configuration fields. config.url: The URL to request data from. The URL can include parameters of the form ((parameter-name)) to be supplied by the matching property. For example, if our url is https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/pokemon/((pokemon)) the value of the URL will be modified by the current value of the property pokemon. config.params: A comma-separated list of query parameters to add to the query string of the URL when making the request. The params should have a matching property defined in the node that contains the value for the parameter. URL Request Example​ OpenAPI Requests​ The OpenAPI form of request take some OpenAPI specification and turns it into an API Request module. The configuration specifies the location of the specification, the version, the request path, and all parameters to include. name: Pokemon API Search description: Search for any pokemon and get its attributes! generate: type: fetch config: # Provide a OpenAPI spec openapi: openapi: 3.0.0 servers: - url: 'https://pokeapi.co/' paths: /api/v2/pokemon/{pokemon}/: get: operationId: pokemon_read # Declare the manifest information here alternatively # x-open: # name: Pokemon API Search # description: Search for any pokemon and get its attributes! parameters: - in: path name: pokemon required: true schema: description: Pokemon name or unique integer value identifying this pokemon. title: Pokemon type: string # Provide custom properties not in the OpenAPI spec via x-open # x-open: # name: ... responses: default: description: Attributes for the pokemon, including their weight, height, abilities and more. content: text/plain: schema: type: string OpenAPI Request Configuration​ type: This must be set to fetch. config: The request configuration. See below for specific OpenAPI request configuration fields. config.openapi: The OpenAPI specific details. See configuration fields below. config.openapi.openapi: The OpenAPI Specification version. config.openapi.servers.url: The location to find the OpenAPI Specifications. config.openapi.paths: The path to request data from. See example below for strtucture. OpenAPI Request Example​ TODO: Needs to be turned into an embed. name: New York Times Article Search # ... other manifest fields generate: type: fetch config: # Provide a OpenAPI spec openapi: openapi: 3.0.0 servers: - url: http://api.nytimes.com/svc/search/v2 - url: https://api.nytimes.com/svc/search/v2 info: # This info.description would be used as the manifest's description description: With the Article Search API, you can search New York Times articles from Sept. 18, 1851 to today, retrieving headlines, abstracts, lead paragraphs, links to associated multimedia and other article metadata. termsOfService: http://developer.nytimes.com/tou title: Article Search API version: 1.0.0 externalDocs: url: http://developer.nytimes.com/ security: - apikey: [] paths: /articlesearch.json: get: description: | Article Search requests use the following URI structure: parameters: - description: Search query term. Search is performed on the article body, headline and byline. in: query name: q required: false schema: type: string # Rename q to query for the property, and provide a name for the property x-open: key: query name: Article Query - description: YYYYMMDD Restricts responses to results with publication dates of the date specified or later. in: query name: begin_date required: false schema: type: string responses: "200": content: application/json: schema: properties: # The first level of objects will all become properties response: properties: docs: items: $ref: "#/components/schemas/Doc" type: array meta: properties: hits: type: integer offset: type: integer time: type: integer type: object type: object type: object description: The docs requested by the article search. x-open: # If provided, we will expose the list/array as a property, and also the first item in the array as a top result. array: path: response.docs # only required if the developer wants to provide a list of results with the top result key: docs # optional, default is result_array name: Articles # optional description: Array of articles that matches the search query. # optional # Note: All property fields are accepted. e.g. order, hidden, default, etc. top: name: Top Article # optional description: Top article object that matches the search query # optional # Note: All property fields are accepted. e.g. top-order, hidden, default, etc. summary: Article Search tags: - Stories components: schemas: Doc: properties: _id: type: string blog: items: {} type: array document_type: description: Document type (article, multimedia). type: string headline: properties: kicker: type: string main: type: string # If specified, will expose nested objects too. By default, only the first level are automatically surfaced. x-top: name: Main Headline # Note: All property fields are accepted. e.g. top-order, hidden, default, etc. type: object type_of_material: description: Type of asset (Correction, News, Op-Ed, Review, Video, ...). type: string word_count: description: Number of words in the article. type: string type: object securitySchemes: apikey: in: query name: api-key type: apiKey

searchDocs.title: Subscriptions
searchDocs.content: Subscriptions It is often important to be made aware of when something changes in Openexus; notably, properties on a module as they change state. This is acheived through the SDK subscription system. Whenever something changes, everything that is subscribed to listen for changes gets notified. Single Subscription​ To listen to a property change, we simply use the context.subscribe() function. context.subscribe() has the signature context.subscribe(<property name>, <subscribe function>). Whenever <property name> changes, <subscribe function> is executed. The <subscribe function> receives the new values, the old value, and the property name as arguments: mySubscribeFunction(newValue, oldValue, propertyName). Here's an example: const sub = context.subscribe('count', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); One can also To stop listening to a property change, simply call unsubscribe() with the same arguments you called subscribe. Here's an example again: const subFunc = (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }; const sub = context.subscribe('count', subFunc); setTimeout(() => { // Stop listening to ((count)) changes after 10s sub.unsubscribe('count', subFunc); }, 10000); VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid src/main.ts const sub = context.subscribe('count', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); setTimeout(() => { // Stop listening to ((count)) changes after 30s sub.unsubscribe(); }, 30000); `} Multiple Subscriptions​ If you need to subscribe to mutliple properties at once, you can pass in an array of property names, instead of a single property name. If any property of the array changes, the <subscriber function> will be called for that property. If multiple properties change, the <subscribed function> will be called one time for each property changed. VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid src/main.js const sub = context.subscribe('count', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); setTimeout(() => { // Stop listening to ((count)) changes after 10s sub.unsubscribe(); }, 10000); `} function callbackFn(path, value) { // should return cell instead of path? } context.subscribe(['property1', 'property2', ...], callbackFn); // subscribe to multiple ports Subscribe to all properties​ Sometimes it is useful to subscribe to all property for a given module at once. This can be accomplished using context.subscribeAll(). context.subscribeAll() has the following signature: context.subscribeAll(<subscriber function>). Whenever any property of the module changes, the subscription will be called. If multiple properties of the module change, a call for each changed properly will be run. VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid src/main.js const sub = context.subscribeAll((value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); setTimeout(() => { // Stop listening to ((count)) changes after 10s sub.unsubscribe(); }, 10000); `} function callbackFn(path, value) { // should return cell instead of path? } context.subscribeAll(callbackFn); Unsubscribing​ As mentioned above one can unsubscribe from a property by passing the same arguments to context.unsubscribe() that were used to make the subscription in the first place. However, it is worth nothing that when you pass an array of property names to context.subscribe() you may either unsubscribe to all of them by passing the same array of property names to context.unsubscribe(), or you may unsubscribe from a single one of the property names in the array at a time by calling context.unsubscribe() with a single property name.
